body: {"status":"ok","message-type":"work-list","message-version":"1.0.0","message":{"facets":{},"total-results":1832117,"items":[{"abstract":"<jats:p>AbstractContent-based image retrieval is the process of retrieving a subset of images from an extensive image gallery based on visual contents, such as color, shape or spatial relations, and texture. In some applications, such as localization, image retrieval is employed as the initial step. In such cases, the accuracy of the top-retrieved images significantly affects the overall system accuracy. The current paper introduces a simple yet efficient image retrieval system with a fewer trainable parameters, which offers acceptable accuracy in top-retrieved images. The proposed method benefits from a dilated residual convolutional neural network with triplet loss. Experimental evaluations show that this model can extract richer information (i.e., high-resolution representations) by enlarging the receptive field, thus improving image retrieval accuracy without increasing the depth or complexity of the model. To enhance the extracted representations\u2019 robustness, the current research obtains candidate regions of interest from each feature map and applies Generalized-Mean pooling to the regions. As the choice of triplets in a triplet-based network affects the model training, we employ a triplet online mining method. We test the performance of the proposed method under various configurations on two of the challenging image-retrieval datasets, namely Revisited Paris6k (RPar) and UKBench. The experimental results show an accuracy of 94.54 and 80.23 (mean precision at rank 10) in the RPar medium and hard modes and 3.86 (recall at rank 4) in the UKBench dataset, However, as all the triplets are treated equally, triplet loss has a bottleneck problem of slow convergence and other unsatisfactory performances. In this article, we propose solutions by appropriately weighting triplets according to the relative similarities among the training samples. Specifically, we present three weighting functions to assign an appropriate weight for the selected informative triplets to accelerate the convergence. We evaluate our approach on two widely used benchmark datasets: Flickr30k and MSCOCO, with results outperforming the previous methods, which demonstrates its Signal Processing Letters"],"is-referenced-by-count":71,"URL":"https:\/\/doi.org\/10.1109\/lsp.2021.3065903","type":"journal-article"},{"abstract":"<jats:p>Matching cross-modality pedestrian images (  i.e  ., visible images and infrared images) has been considered a useful and important application in the person re-identification (reID) field due to its potential to retrieve a person cross daytime and nighttime in real-life practice. However, it is a challenging task. Two main difficulties arise here. 1-Different imaging principle of spectrum cameras leads to a large cross-modality discrepancy between visible images and infrared images. 2-The various views of the large-scale distributed surveillance cameras also result in within-class variations. Along with challenges for the task itself, a strong baseline is also an important integral part of the research field, for the sense that the baseline can be the chief reason for the considerable progress on benchmarks and a strong baseline can evaluate the effectiveness of algorithms fairly. To address the aforementioned issues, this paper first systematically studies the training methods and presents a strong baseline network for the visible-infrared person reID task. Beyond using the existing training methods, we further propose a novel cross-modality contrastive learning (CMCL) scheme, which contains intra-modality contrastive loss and inter-modality contrastive loss, to improve the embedding quality for images of two modalities. Thorough experiments show the superior performance of baseline network and CMCL. For instance, on the RegDB dataset, our work outperforms state-of-the-art values by 7.56% \/ 4.60% on Rank-1 \/ mAP metrics.<\/jats:p>","DOI":"10.2139\/ssrn.3987067","type":"posted-content","is-referenced-by-count":1,"title":["Beyond a Strong Baseline: Cross-Modality Contrastive Learning for Visible-Infrared Person Re-Identification"],"author":[{"given":"Pengfei","family":"FANG","sequence":"first","affiliation":[],"role":[{"vocabulary":"crossref","role":"author"}]},{"given":"Yukang","family":"Zhang","sequence":"additional","affiliation":[],"role":[{"vocabulary":"crossref","role":"author"}]},{"given":"Zhenzhong","family":"Lan","sequence":"additional","affiliation":[],"role":[{"vocabulary":"crossref","role":"author"}]}],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2021]]},"URL":"https:\/\/doi.org\/10.2139\/ssrn.3987067"},{"abstract":"<jats:p>In traditional retrieval systems, text and image queries are processed independently through unimodal methods. However, real-world applications necessitate cross-modal retrieval techniques for better effectiveness. This study proposes a contrastive learning-based approach that integrates BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) and Vision Transformer (ViT) for bidirectional image-caption retrieval. This method demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on the Flickr8K dataset, achieving BLEU and ROUGE-L scores of 0.9397 and 0.9487, respectively. Additionally, we introduce a non-contrastive counterpart utilizing mean squared error (MSE) loss for direct feature matching, which enhances computational efficiency while maintaining competitive performance and higher retrieval accuracy. Our comparative evaluation highlights that, while contrastive learning offers subtle semantic alignment, non-contrastive learning serves as an efficient, computation-driven alternative. These findings provide valuable insights into optimizing vision-language models.<\/jats:p>","DOI":"10.2139\/ssrn.6265287","type":"posted-content","is-referenced-by-count":0,"title":["Bridging Vision and Language: Contrastive vs Non-Contrastive Learning for Image-Caption Retrieval"],"author":[{"given":"Salama","family":"Salim Humaid Tamim","sequence":"first","affiliation":[],"role":[{"role":"author","vocabulary":"crossref"}]},{"ORCID":"https:\/\/orcid.org\/0000-0002-9284-6112","authenticated-orcid":true,"given":"Osman","family":"Abul","sequence":"additional","affiliation":[],"role":[{"role":"author","vocabulary":"crossref"}]},{"given":"Zaher","family":"Al Aghbari","sequence":"additional","affiliation":[],"role":[{"role":"author","vocabulary":"crossref"}]}],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2026]]},"URL":"https:\/\/doi.org\/10.2139\/ssrn.6265287"}],"items-per-page":10,"query":{"start-index":0,"search-terms":null}}}
